description: All-in-one solar street light: a photovoltaic panel and an LED head on a short steel pole

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Short steel lighting pole of constant round section standing on a square bolted base flange, and at the top a single assembly carrying two things: a flat rectangular photovoltaic panel in a slim frame tilted up toward the sky on a stubby mount, and directly below and forward of it a flat slab-shaped LED lamp head, a shallow rectangular box with a plain flat lens on its underside, both held on one short horizontal stub arm off the pole top Materials: Powder-coated pale grey steel pole chalking and streaked with rain, rust weeping from the base flange bolts, dark blue-black solar cells behind glass with a dusty film and bird droppings on the upper edge, pale anodised panel frame, grimy lamp lens with insect debris.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless pure WHITE studio matte. The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless white backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient. This is a studio cut-out, NOT an outdoor photograph: there must be no sky, no clouds, no buildings, no road and no overhead cables anywhere in the frame.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo. The lamp is switched OFF and emits no light.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 1.34 x 4.546 x 0.716 m. Cost: 420 triangles / 8000, 5 draw calls / 6, 2 materials / 4, 5 unique geometries / 8, 2 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.718, 0.874, 0.68], interior hole fractions [0.001, 0.0008, 0.0067, 0.0007]).  Five components at 5 draw calls of a hero ceiling of 6 -- the real cost here is submissions, not triangles (420 of 8000), because the panel, its mount and the head must stay the separate volumes the asset notes require.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 1.340 x 4.546 x 0.716 m against the declared 1.35 x 4.6 x 0.75 -- within 1% on width, 1.2% on height and 4.5% on depth. Width is the panel's -X overhang plus the lamp head's +X, which is exactly how the asset notes describe the figure.

A 0.92 x 0.74 m laminate raked 0.30 rad in an aluminium frame that stands proud of it on all four sides, with the cell grid as a post-construction tile. The previous build was a bare flat plate with no cells, no frame and no strut. Panel 0.74 deep rather than the notes' rough 0.6: the declared envelope depth is 0.75 and the panel is the only thing that can set it -- at 0.6 the measured depth came out 12% under.

A flat slab head with a darker lens plate, on a short arm on the OPPOSITE side of the pole from the panel and 0.64 m below it. The asset notes make exactly that arrangement the identity -- 'those two must stay separate volumes at the right relative sizes' -- and it is now legible from every azimuth.

Two material layers: galvanised steel for pole, gussets, plate, mount and head, and a PV laminate carrying its aluminium frame as a vertex colour. Galvanised luma 162 is clear of the 55.5-60.5 window gatecrop's alpha key erases. The cell tile was rescaled from 0.16 m to 0.55 m: at 0.16 it repeated six times across the panel and its bands read as a venetian blind rather than the 6-9 cells a real panel has. NOT carried: the plate's heavy rust bleed at the foot, which is directional where the tile is isotropic.

A flared foot at r 0.088 tapering to r 0.038 at the head, with four triangular gussets welded up from the baseplate and four bolts on a 0.32 m plate. The previous build was a smooth pipe with none of it; the gussets are what read as a bolted structural post rather than a tube pushed into a plate.

name: Solar LED Street Lamp
nameTh: เสาไฟถนนโซลาร์เซลล์
notes:
The all-in-one solar unit that has appeared on new provincial roads, temple approaches and rural sois over the last decade, where there is no distribution supply to tap. It is unmistakable in silhouette because the tilted panel is the widest thing on the prop and sits above the lamp head, so those two must stay separate volumes at the right relative sizes -- panel roughly 1.0 x 0.6 m, lamp head about 0.5 m long. Sized from a 4.5 m mounting height, which is lower than a mains road column; the pole is about 0.09 m across. budgetClass is the derived large, which is right for a pole, a panel and a head. Static: bolted to a foundation, so physics stays disabled.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED large -> hero (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.
